The case describes an asymptomatic, firm, mobile, non-tender 2.5 cm nuchal mass at the nape of the neck in a patient without systemic B symptoms. Critically, the skin over the nodule *cannot be pinched*, which is a subtle but clinically meaningful physical sign: it suggests dermal or subcutaneous tethering — i.e., the lesion is not freely mobile within the subcutaneous fat plane but is adherent to or involves the dermis or deeper structures (e.g., fascia, muscle, or neurovascular bundle). It frequently demonstrates *skin tethering* — the overlying skin cannot be pinched or moved independently — due to its dermal origin and fibrous capsule adherence. It is often misdiagnosed clinically as a lipoma or lymph node, but its characteristic “tenting” or lack of skin mobility is a recognized physical clue. While imaging and FNA are pending, pilomatrixoma is the *most likely diagnosis* given the constellation of features: nuchal location, firmness, mobility (i.e., not fixed to deep structures), absence of tenderness/inflammation, lack of B symptoms, and — most discriminatively — the inability to pinch the overlying skin. - Firm consistency — consistent with pilomatrixoma’s calcified, fibrotic stroma  
- Mobile (not fixed to deep structures) — pilomatrixomas are typically mobile within the dermis/subcutis

- FNA cytology — to identify basaloid cells, ghost (anucleate) keratinocytes, and calcifications diagnostic of pilomatrixoma

- Presence of overlying skin changes (e.g., bluish discoloration, ulceration) — not reported  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Pilomatrixoma
